rationale: A wins because it does the hard PR work: it turns the same facts into different reporter-shaped stories and names the holes before they embarrass the founder. A's “Substack's video feed raises a question for writers who never wanted to be on camera” finds real tension inside the launch. B has bones, but “Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app” is an unsupported victory lap, and “The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up” argues past the evidence. A pressures the update; B inflates it.
gaps_in_A: “Substack is done being a newsletter company” is punchy but slightly over-declarative; the update supports a media-app push, not a completed identity change.
“subscribers' feeds” is a small grounding wobble; the update says a TikTok-style feed, not specifically subscribers' feeds.
The next step tag “meanest-editor” is awkward workflow residue. The actual useful move is drafting the category angle and preparing the finance answers.
gaps_in_B: “all-in-video media app” invents commitment the facts do not support. Substack added native video and podcasts; it did not become all-in on video.
“native video and the TikTok-style feed are launching now” misstates the peg. The update says video launches now; the feed strategy already existed.
“puts a newsletter platform in the ring with YouTube and TikTok” overreaches without proof that Substack has open discovery, creator scale, or comparable video consumption.
“The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up” reaches a conclusion before doing the math. The facts give scale hints, not a rebuttal to funding concerns.
